text:
The deck of a suspension bridge is not carried directly by the ground at every point; it is a stiffened platform hung from cables. Traffic, the deck’s own weight, and other live loads first enter the deck and its stiffening girder or truss. That stiffening element spreads concentrated loads over a longer length and keeps the deck from deforming too sharply, but it is the hangers that carry the load upward. The hangers are tension members spaced along the bridge, and each one picks up a share of the deck load and transfers it to the main cable above.

The main cables are the principal load-carrying elements. They sag between the towers in a curve, and when the hangers pull downward on them, the cables respond by developing tension. The tension is not simply vertical: because the cable is curved, the tension has both a vertical component, which balances the downward pull from the hangers, and a horizontal component, which is roughly constant along the cable. The vertical component of the cable force supports the deck load, while the horizontal component pulls the cable toward the towers and anchorages.

At each tower, the main cable passes over a saddle or support. The downward pull from the cable is transferred into the tower as compression, so the tower acts like a column carrying the vertical load toward its foundation. The horizontal pull from the main span is balanced by the cable on the other side of the tower, usually a side span or backstay, so the tower does not simply get pulled over. In many bridges the tower also carries some direct deck reactions, but the main cable is the dominant path.

Beyond the towers, the main cables continue to anchorages at the ends of the bridge. These anchorages may be massive concrete blocks, rock anchors, or other ground connections. They hold the ends of the cables and resist the large tension pull, transferring it into the ground or rock. The tower foundations similarly spread the compressive loads into the ground. Thus the overall path is from the deck into the stiffening girder, from the girder into the hangers, from the hangers into the main cables, and from the cables into the towers and anchorages. The towers carry compression down to their foundations, while the anchorages resist cable tension and tie the whole cable system into the ground. In that way, the ground ultimately supports both the downward weight of the bridge and the horizontal pull generated by the suspended cables.
